title: Errands
dek: Every one of these needs a login, a card, an identity check or a human being in a reading room. They are drafted, costed and ordered by what they would settle.
lead: An archive that can only use what is free and unauthenticated will stop at a particular place, and this one has stopped there. What follows is the queue past that point. Each entry says what the source is, what it would settle, and roughly what it costs — so that anyone who wants to help can pick one up without asking what to do.

rows.what: The marriage of John Saniger and Lydia, Berkeley, about 1797 — ANSWERED, and they do not do lookups
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives replied 14 September 2026. Andrew Parry, Senior Archives Assistant: “I'm afraid we don't offer any kind of research service.” He gives two routes instead — the Gloucestershire Family History Society (gfhs.org.uk), whose volunteers do lookups, and Ancestry, which holds the filmed Gloucestershire registers with marriages and banns to 1938. Free access is available at a Gloucestershire library or through GFHS.
rows.cost: a GFHS enquiry, or an Ancestry subscription
rows.settles: Hannah's mother's surname. The FamilySearch shared tree calls her LYDIA JONES and dates the marriage to 1797 at Berkeley, but attaches no record to either claim — John Saniger's profile there carries fourteen sources and every one is a baptism. A Berkeley marriage entry of 1797 would name her, and would settle whether the Lyddya Sinegar aged seventy in Hannah's house in 1841 is her mother.
rows.why: THE LAST UNNAMED PERSON IN THE DIRECT ENGLISH LINE
rows.file: ENQUIRY SENT 13 September 2026, ANSWERED 14 September 2026. The archive office cannot be asked to read a register. The entry is still there and still reachable — the door changed, not the record. The next move is GFHS, drafted and waiting to be sent.

rows.what: The will AND the death duty register of Lieutenant-Colonel Joseph D'Arcy, proved 1848
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew — Prerogative Court of Canterbury (PROB 11), and Death Duty Register IR 26, indexed at IR 27/284
rows.settles: Joseph D'Arcy was baptised at Portsea in March 1780, son of Robert and Jean, and died at Homestead, Lymington on 7 February 1848. A newspaper of 3 April 1848 reports that he made his will in February 1844 and begins to summarise it, and the digitised text breaks off. The will names his legatees — which means his children, and possibly his brothers and sisters. It is the closest thing to a family document this line has. AND THERE IS NOW A SECOND DOCUMENT. The Index to Death Duty Registers 1796-1903 has him: JOSEPH D'ARCY of Lymington, Hampshire, grant year 1848, court “PCC and Country Courts”, archive reference IR 27/284. The register behind that index states what the estate was worth and names the legatees and executors — frequently in more detail than the will itself.
rows.why: THE NEAREST THING TO A FAMILY DOCUMENT IN THE ENGLISH LINE
rows.file: index reference found on FindMyPast, 14 September 2026; neither document read

rows.what: RCB Library, Dublin — surviving Church of Ireland registers for Co. Wicklow — ENQUIRY SENT
rows.where: Representative Church Body Library, library@rcbcoi.org — written 13 September 2026, awaiting reply
rows.settles: Which Wicklow Anglican registers survive 1815–1825, whether any are still in parish custody, and whether Betham's marriage licence bond abstracts are worth pursuing. The only live route to the marriage of George Pitt D'Arcy and Maria White.
rows.file: ENQUIRY SENT 13 September 2026. Asked which Wicklow Anglican registers survive for 1815–1825 and in whose custody, whether a list exists that can be consulted from abroad, and whether Betham's marriage licence bond abstracts are worth pursuing for a Dublin-diocese marriage of this date.

rows.what: Bristol Archives — St James marriage of Thomas Sanigre and Martha Golding, 24 August 1828 — ENQUIRY SENT
rows.where: Bristol Archives, archives@bristol.gov.uk — written 13 September 2026, awaiting reply. Their research service is £13 for up to half an hour.
rows.settles: The father's name on that entry would prove in one line that Hannah Saniger's brother is the Thomas Sinegar of Oxford Road. Everything about the identification agrees and nothing documents it.
rows.file: ENQUIRY SENT 13 September 2026. Asked for the fathers' names, abodes, ages, conditions, occupations and witnesses on the entry, and whether it was by banns or licence. The letter lists the nineteen spellings of this surname found so far, because twice already a spelling has been the only thing hiding a record.

rows.what: The Bristol St James register entry for Thomas Sanigre and Martha Golding, 24 August 1828
rows.where: Bristol Archives, or Ancestry's Bristol Church of England Marriages and Banns 1754-1938
rows.settles: The marriage itself is now documented, free, in the FamilySearch index — but that index names no fathers. The original entry would name Thomas's, and prove in one line that Hannah's brother is the Thomas Sinegar of Oxford Road.
rows.file: marriage confirmed 13 September 2026; father's name still unseen

rows.what: Surviving Church of Ireland registers for County Wicklow, and Betham's marriage licence bond abstracts
rows.where: Representative Church Body Library, Dublin; and the National Archives of Ireland
rows.settles: The marriage of George Pitt D'Arcy and Maria White, about 1819. Every Wicklow marriage index reachable online is Roman Catholic, and he was an Anglican officer — the Church of Ireland registers for the county went in the 1922 Four Courts fire. The RCB Library keeps what survived and knows which parishes kept their own books. Betham's abstracts of marriage licence bonds survive even though the bonds burned. THE LICENCE-BOND HALF IS NOW ANSWERED AND IT IS NEGATIVE. FindMyPast's Ireland Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage Licence Bonds Indexes 1623-1866 holds no George D'Arcy at all, and its Dublin diocese entries effectively stop in 1741 — the latest in the whole set are one 1813, one 1752, and then a wall of 1741. Betham's Prerogative Marriage Licences Abstracts ends at 1810. Neither can hold an 1819 marriage. What remains is the RCB Library's question about surviving parish custody.
rows.file: licence bonds searched and ruled out by date, 14 September 2026

rows.what: Gloucestershire wills for the Saniger line — ANSWERED, and the answer is that there are none
rows.where: Searched on FindMyPast: Gloucestershire Wills & Administrations 1801-1858 (Consistory Court of Gloucester, 14,195 entries)
rows.settles: Read under wildcards SAN*, SIN*, SYN* and SWA*, which return every form this surname takes. The whole index holds two Saniger-variant entries: ABRAHAM SYNEGAR, cardmaker of Dursley, administration 1813/8; and JOHN SANIGAR, carpenter of Oldbury-on-Severn in Thornbury, will 1822/194. Neither is Berkeley. John Saniger of Berkeley left no proved will and no administration in the diocesan court, so this route to naming his children is closed rather than merely unopened. Control: SMITH returns 277.
rows.why: CLOSED 14 SEPTEMBER 2026

rows.what: The marriage of Thomas Sinegar and Martha, Gloucestershire, about 1829
rows.where: Bristol Archives or Gloucestershire Archives — not in any online index searched
rows.settles: Whether Hannah Saniger had a brother living a mile from her in Bristol. Thomas Saniger, baptised at Berkeley 3 July 1808 son of John, is exactly the age and birthplace of the Thomas Sinegar at 7 Oxford Road in 1851 — and a Gloucestershire marriage entry names the father, as his son's did in 1871. Everything else about the identification lines up and nothing documents it.
rows.why: TURNS THE STRONGEST INFERENCE HERE INTO A FACT

rows.what: Chew Magna, Somerset — the parish register, 1795–1820
rows.where: Somerset Heritage Centre, Taunton; filmed, and on the subscription sites
rows.settles: Where Hannah Saniger was born. A Saniger family living two streets from the Wakefields in 1851 gives its birthplace as Chew Magna, and Chew Magna is in SOMERSET — which is the one thing the 1841 census insists on about Hannah and about the Lyddya Sinegar in her house. FreeREG's Chew Magna transcript is a fragment of two Smith entries in twenty-one years, so this cannot be searched from a desk. A baptism for Hannah Saniger, daughter of John and Lydia, would close the oldest open question on this site in one line.
rows.why: THE BEST LEAD THIS ARCHIVE HAS EVER HAD ON HANNAH

rows.what: Samuel Sneyd's death certificate, Hanley 1855 — LOCAL REFERENCE FOUND
rows.where: General Register Office (GRO 1855 Q3, Stoke, vol 6b p.75) OR, better, Stoke-on-Trent Register Office against the local reference HAN/011/023, found 15 September 2026 in the free Staffordshire BMD index. That index also gives his age at death as 77, independently confirming the Hanley burial register.
rows.settles: The exact day, the cause, and the informant — who is usually the widow or a son, named with their address. It would confirm 20 September as the day of death and put a name to whoever registered it.

rows.what: The Peculiar of Chew — probate for Chew Magna, and what survives of Somerset wills
rows.where: Somerset Heritage Centre, Taunton
rows.settles: Chew Magna was a PECULIAR, outside the bishop's ordinary jurisdiction, proving its own wills down to 1787 — so Chew Magna probate is not where a researcher would first look for it. Before anyone is sent to Taunton, the archive should establish what survives of Somerset probate at all, and under which court a Chew Magna will of the 1820s would be found.
rows.file: jurisdiction identified 13 September 2026, Collinson and TNA Discovery

rows.what: GRO birth certificate — Miriam Wakefield, Jun quarter 1840, Bristol, vol 11 page 183
rows.where: General Register Office, gro.gov.uk (an account, no visit)
rows.settles: It names her mother WITH HER MAIDEN SURNAME. Five Queensland death registrations now say Saniger in four spellings, so the name itself is settled — but not one English record has ever confirmed it, and the 1841 census says Hannah was born OUTSIDE Gloucestershire, which is why no Gloucestershire register will ever find her. This certificate is the only document identified that attacks the question from the English end.
rows.why: THE CHEAPEST DECISIVE DOCUMENT ON THIS SITE

rows.what: Run the NSW BDM historical index for the D'Arcys
rows.where: familyhistory.bdm.nsw.gov.au — free to search
rows.cost: free, ten minutes, but behind a bot check
rows.settles: The entire D'Arcy side were New South Welshmen. George Pitt D'Arcy died at Parramatta in 1849, George Lindsay was born there in 1829, Frederick Robert and Charlotte both crossed. NSW death registrations name the parents of the deceased — which is how Queensland's index settled the Saniger name five times over. This is the largest free index this archive has never searched, and it is shut to an automated browser.
rows.why: THE BIGGEST FREE THING LEFT

rows.what: Search irishgenealogy.ie for the Creech, Atkinson and Mulcahy lines
rows.where: irishgenealogy.ie — free, no login
rows.settles: This archive has three Irish lines and has never searched an Irish record. The most testable claim is the marriage of Paul Cole Atkinson and Jane Creech at Carrigaline, County Cork, on 27 September 1853, which the site states as fact and has never seen. Then Richard Atkinson of Limerick, and Catherine Margaret Mulcahy of Cork, whose parents are unknown.
rows.why: THREE LINES, ONE FREE DATABASE

rows.what: PROB 11/1991/312 — the will of John Maddock Jones of Ruabon
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew — digitised — The image is DIGITISED and the record page reads “£3.50 - sign in to get this free”. It is not a paywall but a free registration: a TNA account costs nothing and the PDF then downloads at no charge. Checked 14 September 2026. The on-page preview is watermarked, with “to download this record without a watermark, please add it to your basket”, so the sign-in is the route.
rows.cost: free, with a free TNA account
rows.settles: He married Margarett Maria Isabella D'Arcy, Robert and Jean's daughter, at Chatham in 1806 by licence, witnessed by her brother Joseph. His will of 1844 would name his widow and children — an entire Welsh branch of this family that the archive has never contained a word about. Also not on FindMyPast, for the same reason as errand 20: its Prerogative Court of Canterbury wills index stops at 1800.
rows.why: A WHOLE BRANCH, FOR THREE POUNDS

rows.what: The Berkeley estate deeds, D2957/41, at Gloucestershire Archives
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives
rows.settles: The Saniger family in its own parish, by name and holding, from 1601 to 1749 — John Saniger yeoman, Edward Saniger of Saniger gent and clothier, Maurice Saniger and Jane his wife. This is the documentary spine of the family the archive has only ever seen through a parish register that stops in 1677.

rows.what: Hinton manor court rolls, GCR/231 and 258, 1523–1528
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives / Berkeley Castle Muniments
rows.settles: Saniger lies in the tithing of Hinton. Manor court rolls list tenants by name at each court — the one record type that catches a family holding land in a parish whose register is lost to us after 1677.

rows.what: Twelve named RG 4 Bristol chapel registers — the birth/baptism volumes that cover 1805–1815
rows.where: The National Archives, RG 4 — NOT digitised on TNA's own site; published through commercial partners
rows.cost: a visit, or a digitised copy via a subscription site
rows.settles: Where Hannah Saniger was born, if she was born to a chapel-going family. The catalogue has now been read properly: there are THIRTY-SIX Bristol registers in RG 4, not five, and exactly twelve of them are births or baptisms whose dates cover her window. Broad Mead Baptist births 1787–1817 (RG 4/2697) and Lewins Mead Presbyterian baptisms 1718–1840 (RG 4/1830) each cover it on their own. Access corrected 13 September 2026: all twelve are marked digitised:false at Kew, so this needs a subscription or a visit, not an afternoon.

rows.what: Lichfield Bishop's Transcripts for Madeley, 1740s
rows.where: Staffordshire Record Office / Lichfield — Staffordshire Name Indexes was tested on 14 September 2026 and cannot help: it holds twenty-six collections and no parish registers or bishop's transcripts at all. Its Lichfield wills index, searched at the same time, has no Sneyd of Madeley among thirty-six.
rows.settles: The baptism of William Sneyd the weaver, about 1746. FreeREG holds no Bishop's Transcripts for Madeley at all, and his baptism is not in any transcribed Staffordshire register. The diocesan second copy is the obvious next place and nobody has asked for it.

rows.what: PROB 11/1728/64 — the will of Major-General Robert D'Arcy
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew — The image is DIGITISED and the record page reads “£3.50 - sign in to get this free”. It is not a paywall but a free registration: a TNA account costs nothing and the PDF then downloads at no charge. Checked 14 September 2026. The on-page preview is watermarked, with “to download this record without a watermark, please add it to your basket”, so the sign-in is the route.
rows.cost: free, with a free TNA account
rows.settles: His parentage is the largest open question on this site and no record of his life names a father. A will names family. Found 9 September 2026 and still unordered. CHECKED ON FINDMYPAST WHILE THE TRIAL WAS OPEN AND IT IS NOT THERE. FindMyPast's only Prerogative Court of Canterbury collections are a wills index for 1750-1800 and an administrations index for 1660-1700. Nothing in its catalogue carries PCC wills proved after 1800, so this will, Joseph's of 1848 and John Maddock Jones's of 1844 are all beyond it. £3.50 at Kew is the price and there is no free substitute.
rows.why: THE PRIORITY
rows.file: FindMyPast coverage checked and excluded, 14 September 2026

rows.what: Enquiry to the Royal Engineers Museum, Chatham
rows.where: The Corps' own archive
rows.settles: Robert D'Arcy's parentage, from the records of the Corps he served for fifty-one years and the town he died in.
rows.why: The best chance of closing the question the archive was built around

rows.what: Three Queensland death certificates
rows.where: Queensland Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages
rows.settles: Three causes of death, and three sets of parents named in a civil record rather than a tree. Registration numbers already identified.
rows.why: Turns three dotted pedigree edges solid

rows.what: Two Chatham burials
rows.where: Medway Archives
rows.settles: Robert D'Arcy, 1827, and Constantine D'Arcy, 1805. A burial register can give an age, an abode and sometimes a relationship.
rows.why: The likeliest of all of these to succeed

rows.what: Where Arthur Hartley Sneyd is commemorated — DONE, and the archive was right
rows.where: Commonwealth War Graves Commission, casualty 1451888. Reached 14 September 2026 at the third attempt: the Azure bot check cleared by itself in a real browser after a few seconds.
rows.settles: Confirmed outright, from the authority rather than by inference from the B.2090A's “Not yet to hand”: Private ARTHUR HARTLEY SNEYD, service number 5050, 9th Bn. Australian Infantry, A.I.F., died 20 August 1916 aged 22, commemorated on the VILLERS-BRETONNEUX MEMORIAL, Somme — the memorial to the missing, which carries 10,696 names. CWGC adds: “Son of Arthur and Martha Sneyd, of James St., Wooloowin, Brisbane. Born at Rockhampton, Queensland.” Every one of those details was already held here. The record corrected nothing and confirmed everything, which is the rarer and duller of the two outcomes.
rows.why: CONFIRMED, NOT CORRECTED

rows.what: The generation above Francis Murdoch
rows.where: ScotlandsPeople
rows.settles: The Ayrshire Murdochs are a quarter of the tested descendant and the archive has 25 of 52 ancestor slots filled. The DNA points straight at this gap.
rows.why: The branch the archive has most neglected

rows.what: Richard Atkinson and Anne, of Limerick
rows.where: RootsIreland
rows.settles: Anything at all. The Atkinsons are five generations deep and stop dead at the emigrant.

rows.what: Nine Queensland State Archives items
rows.where: Queensland State Archives, Runcorn
rows.settles: Arthur Hartley Sneyd's 1916 intestacy; William Hartley Sneyd's 1873 insolvency — a wholly new fact; four wills, one of which may be the gaol governor's; two police staff files that are probably his sons.
rows.why: All nine identified to series and file number

rows.what: Which Ordnance series carries a Royal Engineers commission of 1776 — ANSWERED: WO 54/240
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew. WO 54/240, “Engineers”, 1755–1780 — the Board of Ordnance commission book, and the ONLY engineers volume in that run covering the 1770s (the next begins in 1797). Corroborate from WO 47/87 and WO 47/88, the Board's minutes for the two halves of 1776, where the decision to appoint would be minuted and dated. WO 54/939–945 holds original instruments of appointment, 1670–1885.
rows.cost: a visit — none of it is digitised or name-indexed
rows.settles: Robert D'Arcy was appointed by the BOARD OF ORDNANCE, not commissioned by the War Office and not by purchase, which is why the ordinary officer series have never held him. It would also settle 1776 against 1778: Connolly's Roll gives one date and the Army Lists another, and this archive currently prints both on different pages.
rows.why: THE SERIES IS NAMED AT LAST
rows.file: ANSWERED 15 September 2026 from TNA's own guides and catalogue. Note the warning in the Board of Ordnance guide: “you cannot search this series by a person's name in our online catalogue”. WO 25/3913, Royal Engineers officers' services, IS digitised and name-indexed — but begins in 1796, so it holds him only if he was still serving.

rows.what: PROB 11/1825/326 — the will of Elizabeth Saniger, widow of Thornbury
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew — digitised, downloadable — The image is DIGITISED and the record page reads “£3.50 - sign in to get this free”. It is not a paywall but a free registration: a TNA account costs nothing and the PDF then downloads at no charge. Checked 14 September 2026. The on-page preview is watermarked, with “to download this record without a watermark, please add it to your basket”, so the sign-in is the route.
rows.cost: free, with a free TNA account
rows.settles: A widow's will names her children. This one was proved on 24 December 1833, in a parish between Berkeley and Bristol that holds eight Saniger register entries, at exactly the moment Hannah Saniger was a married woman with children in Bristol. Probate is the record type this archive has never once searched for this surname, and this is the first thing it turned up.
rows.why: A WIDOW'S WILL NAMES HER CHILDREN — AND IT IS FREE

rows.what: Portsea St Mary's register itself, 1770–1800 — baptisms, marriages and burials
rows.where: Portsmouth History Centre; filmed and also on the subscription sites
rows.cost: a reading ticket, or a subscription
rows.settles: Whether Robert and Jean D'Arcy had other children at Portsea. FreeREG's transcript of this parish is TWENTY-TWO MONTHS long — baptisms for 1780 and 1781 and almost nothing else — so Joseph's entry survives by luck and the silence around it means nothing at all. A thirty-year run of the original volume would test the whole household, and might name Robert's own marriage.
rows.why: THE ARCHIVE'S OLDEST ENGLISH FIND IS STANDING ON TWO YEARS

rows.what: Smyth of Nibley, Men and Armour for Gloucestershire, 1608 — DONE, and it gave eleven men
rows.where: Read 14 September 2026 in the online transcript of the 1902 edition at coaley.net/glos1608. The 1980 facsimile on the Internet Archive is a lending item and returns HTTP 401 without an account.
rows.cost: a library, or a secondhand copy
rows.settles: Eleven men of the surname in four spellings — Saniger (5), Sanyger (3), Syniger (2), Sainger (1). One of them, JOHN SAINGER, weaver, is mustered inside the hamlet itself, which the survey writes as “Saniger [in Hinton parish, Berkeley]”. Two of the four spellings were not among the seventeen this archive held. Every 1608 form ends -GER, which dates the -GAR forms of the later registers as late rather than old.
rows.why: THE SURNAME, DOCUMENTED TWO CENTURIES BEFORE THE REGISTERS
rows.file: DONE 14 September 2026. No descent is claimed: nothing links these eleven to Hannah Saniger. What it gives is the surname's home ground and its trades.

rows.what: D2957/41 and D3831/Box5/1 — the Saniger and Panthurst deeds
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives, Alvin Street, Gloucester
rows.cost: a visit, or a copy order
rows.settles: The catalogue descriptions alone give six generations of names, trades and land. The deeds themselves give witnesses, relationships and often the words “son and heir”. D3831/Box5/1 is a century of Panthurst Farm, 1716–1814 — the farm John Saniger sold into in 1601.

rows.what: The parish register of ST MICHAEL, BARBADOS, 1780s — the original, not the index
rows.where: Barbados Department of Archives, Black Rock, St Michael; the register is filmed by FamilySearch as film 1157925
rows.cost: an enquiry, or a FamilySearch affiliate library
rows.settles: The index gives two christenings to Robert D'Arcy and Jane — Constantine on 18 February 1786 and Jane on 17 March 1788 — and nothing else. The register page itself would give the father's rank and corps, the abode, and any further children of the same parents. It is the only direct evidence this archive has that Robert D'Arcy was ever in the West Indies, and it would turn a strong inference into a documented posting.
rows.why: THE ONLY RECORD OF ROBERT D'ARCY BETWEEN 1778 AND 1802

rows.what: Royal Engineers station returns for Barbados and the Leeward Islands, 1783–1790
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew — WO 55 (Ordnance Office, Engineer Papers) and the Royal Engineers Museum, Chatham
rows.settles: When Robert D'Arcy went to Barbados, how long he stayed and in what capacity. His career was long blank between his commission of 17 January 1776 and his majority of 1802, and two christenings are the only things known to fall inside them.

rows.what: British consular death registrations at Le Havre, February and March 1843
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew — RG 35, GRO Miscellaneous Foreign Death Returns, 1830–1921. The France run is RG 35/8–13; on dates, February–March 1843 could only fall in RG 35/8, /9, /10 or /13. The catalogue describes them only as “Part 1…Part 5” — no town, no consulate, no names. The gating finding aid is RG 43/4, Index to RG 35/1-25 Deaths, 1830–1880, which IS digitised but only through paid sites (or free onsite at Kew).
rows.settles: Margaret Jones née D'Arcy died at Havre in February 1843 and her husband Major John Maddock Jones at Ingouville in March. A consular death registration gives an age and frequently a parentage. It is the nearest thing to a birth date for a daughter of Robert D'Arcy.
rows.why: AN AGE FOR ONE OF ROBERT'S CHILDREN
rows.file: SERIES IDENTIFIED 15 September 2026. Two honest limits: the word in the title is MISCELLANEOUS — these are returns that happened to reach the GRO, not a complete register of British deaths in France — so a negative in RG 43/4 would prove only that the death is not in RG 35, not that it went unregistered. And there is no TNA series of French consular death registers for the 1840s at all; FO 27 holds Havre consular correspondence, but it is correspondence, not a register, and is not name-indexed.

rows.what: The death of LYDIA SANIGER at Berkeley, 7 July 1851 — LOCATED, under SANIGAR
rows.where: Found 14 September 2026 in the Gloucestershire Registration Service Index (free, ww3.gloucestershire.gov.uk/bmd): LYDIA SANIGAR, 1851, register 3, entry 265. The certificate is ordered from Gloucestershire against that local reference rather than from the GRO against the quarterly index.
rows.settles: This archive's own tree gives Hannah Saniger's mother as LYDIA JONES, born 13 March 1770 at Wotton-under-Edge and died 7 July 1851 at Berkeley. A death in July 1851 is inside civil registration: the September quarter of the Thornbury district index should hold her, and the certificate gives an age, an occupation of husband and an informant — very often a child. It is the cheapest unexploited document in this archive.
rows.why: THE CERTIFICATE IS NOW ORDERABLE
rows.file: LOCATED 14 September 2026. Invisible under SANIGER, present under SANIGAR — the fourth time a spelling has hidden a record in this family. Coverage checked first: Thornbury/Berkeley deaths are complete 1837-1948.

rows.what: The baptism of Lydia Jones at WOTTON-UNDER-EDGE, about 13 March 1770 — TESTED, and FreeREG cannot answer it
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives. FreeREG was tested on 14 September 2026 and is not a route: it lists Wotton-under-Edge among its places but holds nought Jones entries there of any type between 1740 and 1800. The register itself is filmed and on Ancestry, which Gloucestershire Archives confirmed on the same day holds the county's baptisms to 1913.
rows.settles: Whether JONES is her surname at all, which this site has called an unevidenced assertion for a week while holding a parish and a date for it.
rows.file: TESTED 14 September 2026. Control: 164 Jones baptisms in Gloucestershire 1760-1785 on the same search, so the failure is the parish's transcription, not the query. This is an EMPTY, not a null.

rows.what: CATHERINE COTTON at Berkeley — marriage 10 April 1769, burial 27 September 1778
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives — Berkeley St Mary the Virgin registers (the online transcript stops in 1677)
rows.settles: Her marriage to Thomas Saniger and her burial nine years later, both at Berkeley, both given by this archive's tree with full dates and neither ever requested. She is listed among the open questions as “where did Catherine Cotton come from?” while the answer — Berkeley, born 11 October 1746, daughter of Edward Cotton and Elizabeth — sits in the data files.

rows.what: De Lancey's Brigade muster and commission rolls, 1 June 1778 — for a CONSTANTINE D'ARCY
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew (AO 12/13, Loyalist claims); New York Public Library and the Sir Guy Carleton Papers
rows.settles: This archive's tree gives Robert D'Arcy a BROTHER — Constantine D'Arcy, born Barbados 1759, died Chatham 1778, appointed to De Lancey's Brigade on 1 June 1778, with the note that the original transcription read “Cornelius Dersey”. If that officer is real he is the first sibling ever attached to Robert, and his papers would name their parents. If he is not, the tree has duplicated Robert's own son and back-dated him twenty-seven years, and that needs saying.
rows.why: THE FIRST LEAD ON ROBERT'S PARENTAGE THAT IS NOT THE HOLDERNESS STORY
rows.file: found in this archive's own data 14 September 2026; never tested

rows.what: The Sussex deaths of JANE, CATHERINE and CHARLOTTE D'ARCY — DONE, and what it opened
rows.where: General Register Office (all three are inside civil registration); and the 1841–1871 censuses for Brighton and Falmer
rows.settles: ALL THREE DEATH REGISTRATIONS FOUND, 14 September 2026. Charlotte, aged 73, Brighton Q2 1869, vol 2B p.152; Jane, aged 87, Brighton Q1 1875, vol 2B p.203; Catherine, aged 86, Brighton Q1 1876, vol 2B p.164. Catherine also has a newspaper notice giving her address as Bedford Square and the title MISS, and all three appear in one household in the 1841 Brighton census. What remains is the probate, the certificates themselves, and the gap in 1851–1871.
rows.why: LARGELY CLOSED 14 SEPTEMBER 2026
rows.file: three registrations, an obituary, a probate index entry and a census household

rows.what: IR 26 — the Death Duty register behind IR 27/396, for CATHERINE D'ARCY of Brighton, 1876 — NARROWED TO SEVEN PIECES
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew. IR 26 runs 1796–1903 and IS catalogued to piece level for 1876. The index entry sits in IR 27/396/3 (CHO–DZ); the folio number it gives picks exactly one of the 1876 will registers for surnames C–D: IR 26/2941 (folios 1–251), /2942 (253–503), /2943 (505–749), /2944 (751–1001), /2945 (1003–1253), /2946 (1255–1445), /2947 (1447–1661). If the estate was an administration rather than a will, the 1876 intestate registers (IR 26/3390, /3392) or the succession registers (IR 26/5507–5537) instead.
rows.cost: a visit; none of it is digitised
rows.settles: Catherine D'Arcy died at Bedford Square, Brighton in January 1876 leaving an estate that attracted duty. The Death Duty register states its value and names the executors and the legatees. Three unmarried sisters who outlived their brothers leave their money to nephews and nieces — which is to say, this is the document most likely to name the next generation of this family in England, including anyone descended from Joseph at Lymington.
rows.why: THE MOST LIKELY DOCUMENT TO NAME THE ENGLISH FAMILY AFTER 1850
rows.file: NARROWED 15 September 2026. A belief worth correcting: IR 26 is often said to stop in 1857. It does not — 1857 is where the MICROFILMING stops, not the records. The registers for 1858–1903 survive as originals at Kew, unfilmed and not online, and may need advance notice to produce.

rows.what: Three GRO death certificates — Charlotte 1869, Jane 1875, Catherine 1876, Brighton
rows.where: General Register Office; references in hand (2B/152, 2B/203, 2B/164)
rows.settles: A death certificate gives the exact date, the address, the cause, and the INFORMANT — who for an unmarried woman of 87 is usually the relative who was present. Three certificates would give three informants, and the informants are the point.

rows.what: Jane, Catherine and Charlotte D'Arcy in the 1861 census — 1851 FOUND, 1861 still missing
rows.where: Any census index — but not under a surname beginning D and ending ARCY, which has been searched — and FreeCEN, free and never previously used for this county, was searched on 15 September 2026 with the same result: no D'Arcy of any spelling and any age. Its six Sussex DARCYs are one Kemp Town household, all born in Sussex between 1816 and 1857. What that does NOT establish is how complete FreeCEN's Brighton is for 1861; it narrows the errand without closing it.
rows.settles: 1851 IS DONE: all three are at WESTERN COTTAGE, BRIGHTON, HO107/1646 f.357 p.59 sch.172, indexed under the surname ARCY with the D' lost — which is why every D*ARCY search missed them. 1861 has since been searched four ways — by surname (ARCY and D*ARCY, Sussex), by address (Bedford Square and the Western streets), by birthplace within Sussex (33 people born Barbadoes, read one by one) and by birthplace nationally (25 Janes and 16 Catherines) — and they are in none of it. What is left is a street-by-street read of the 1861 and 1871 enumerators' books for the western end of Brighton, and the Brighton Standard's house-by-house occupancy lists.
rows.why: 1851 CLOSED 14 SEPTEMBER 2026; 1861 SEARCHED FOUR WAYS AND EMPTY
rows.file: the surname was indexed as ARCY — the D' had been read as part of the forename

rows.what: The 422 ARIENZO registers on Antenati — read page by page
rows.where: Portale Antenati, Archivio di Stato di Caserta — free, digitised, and not name-indexed
rows.cost: free, and a great many hours
rows.settles: The Italian side of the marriage that joins this archive to the Falco one. 63 MATRIMONI PROCESSETTI are the prize: the processetti carry birth extracts and parental consents for both parties, which is two generations per marriage. Control-tested — a search for RUSSO at Arienzo returns nothing, so the index is missing, not the family. THIS IS THE FALCO ARCHIVE'S WORK rather than this one's, and is listed here because this archive established the coverage.

rows.what: The Limerick line in CHURCH OF IRELAND records — Atkinson, Cole, Creech, Kent, Bowen, Peevers
rows.where: RCB Library Dublin, and the Representative Church Body's parish holdings for St Mary's, Limerick; RootsIreland by subscription
rows.settles: Five generations that stop dead at the emigrant. The NLI cannot help — it holds CATHOLIC registers and this line is Anglican, on the evidence of ST MARY'S, LIMERICK and the surnames. irishgenealogy.ie is behind a bot check. What is left is the RCB Library, which has already been written to once about Wicklow and could be asked about Limerick in the same letter.
rows.why: THE OLDEST IRISH LINE, AND THE LEAST SEARCHED
rows.file: coverage established 15 September 2026 — the NLI is the wrong denomination

rows.what: BillionGraves, when its search API is answering again
rows.where: billiongraves.com
rows.settles: A second opinion on the Queensland burials, and GPS coordinates Find a Grave does not carry for every plot. Nothing has been searched: the site's own API answered 403 and 400 and the page never finished loading. This is a retry, not a result.

rows.what: Put the HORNBY CLAIM and the KEELE GRAFT to RootsChat
rows.where: rootschat.com — free, and requires a registered account to search or post
rows.cost: a registration, and the patience to answer follow-ups
rows.settles: Contested descents from named families are exactly what forum specialists carry primary knowledge of, and somebody there has usually already read the wills. Two questions are ready to ask, and both should be put as the archive states them, with the evidence, inviting refutation: (1) the Holderness descent — the tree points at the 4th Earl in a note and hangs Robert off a “Thomas (Francis) D'Arcy” in its structure, and neither carries a document; (2) the Keele graft — the descent from Ralph Sneyd of Keele Hall, already DISPROVED here from the Madeley register, where the 1742 baptism names the father as William and Ralph was eighteen. Ask what would break each, not what would confirm it.
rows.why: THE TWO CLAIMS THIS ARCHIVE CANNOT SETTLE ALONE
rows.file: blocked 15 September 2026 — searching the forum requires an account, and none was created

rows.what: The New South Wales marriage certificate of CHARLOTTE CATHCART D'ARCY and ROBERT MEAD PEARSON, Parramatta 1859, registration 2618
rows.where: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths & Marriages
rows.settles: Whether the Charlotte D'Arcy christened at Chatham on 31 March 1826 — eight days before the convict ship England sailed with her father's detachment — is the Charlotte who married at Parramatta thirty-three years later. A New South Wales marriage certificate names both fathers. The circumstantial case is strong: the right age, and the town where George Pitt D'Arcy died in 1849. The middle name is the problem — CATHCART in one index entry, CATHERINE in another, and absent from the baptism.
rows.why: THE LAST OF GEORGE PITT D'ARCY'S CHILDREN UNACCOUNTED FOR

rows.what: Gloucestershire Family History Society — the lookup Gloucestershire Archives cannot do
rows.where: gfhs.org.uk/contact-us — recommended by name by Gloucestershire Archives on 14 September 2026. Volunteer lookups; membership is modest and gives access to their own indexes.
rows.settles: The marriage of JOHN SANIGER and LYDIA at Berkeley, about 1797, and with it the surname of the last unnamed person in the direct English line. The same enquiry can carry the second question: whether Berkeley's register supports Hannah Sanigor's baptism of 18 August 1804 against the family record's 23 July 1805.
rows.why: THE ROUTE THE COUNTY ARCHIVE ITSELF POINTED TO
rows.file: Drafted and not sent — sending mail is David's call. The letter should carry the eighteen spellings found so far, because twice now a spelling has been the thing hiding a record, and a third time in 1608.

rows.what: GDR/B4/1/387 — Christian Saniger v. Mary Millard, defamation, 1768
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives — Gloucester Diocese consistory court
rows.cost: a visit, or a paid copy
rows.settles: Church-court defamation suits are brought by named people about named people, and the depositions give ages, abodes and occupations for every witness. A Saniger suing in 1768 sits exactly in the generation above John Saniger of Berkeley, who married Lydia about 1797 and is the last unnamed link in the direct English line.
rows.why: THE RICHEST UNREAD DOCUMENT FOUND THIS WEEK
rows.file: Found in TNA Discovery, 14 September 2026. Not digitised. Christian is a woman's forename in this period.

rows.what: The three unitemised Berkeley Castle groupings for Saniger — ANSWERED, and they were never unitemised
rows.where: The National Archives' Discovery catalogue itemises the Berkeley Castle Muniments deed by deed — party, land, rent, witnesses, and the GC number to quote when requesting the document. Free, and no account needed. Found 15 September 2026.
rows.cost: an application to the muniment room
rows.settles: A purparty is a share of an inherited estate divided between coheirs — which is precisely what happened when John Swonhungre died without issue in 1401 and his sisters Isabel and Elizabeth took the lands. These three groupings are the paper of that division and of what came after. ANSWERED: 178 records under the medieval spellings, of which 25 were read closely and six carry kinship statements new to this archive.
rows.file: Named but not itemised in TNA Discovery, 14 September 2026.

rows.what: The twenty-five unread page references under “Swanhunger” in Smyth's own index
rows.where: A Description of the Hundred of Berkeley, 1885 edition — free on the Internet Archive
rows.settles: Smyth indexes Swanhunger at pages 130, 232, 253, 280, 286-289, 303, 315, 351, 363-366, 370-371, 374-375, 379-383. Only four have been read. The rest are descriptions of Wanswell, Hame and Nibley in which the family appears as neighbours, tenants and parties.
rows.file: Achievable without leaving the desk; the text is already downloaded.

rows.what: Smyth's citation list for the Swonhunger pedigree — TESTED against the printed Calendars, and they are NOT royal inquisitions
rows.where: Tested 15 September 2026 in the printed Calendars of Inquisitions Post Mortem, volumes 5 to 8 (Edward II to Edward III), free on the Internet Archive. No Swonhunger of any spelling, and no Thomas de Stone. The controls hold: Gloucester appears 230 to 334 times a volume and Berkeley 15 to 17, and a fragment search on “hungr” and “hunge” does return other names — Gravenhunger in Shropshire, Clehungre in Herefordshire — so the search reaches names of that shape and these two families are simply not in them.
rows.cost: a search of the IPM calendars, much of which is in print and free
rows.settles: The reason is structural, and it changes what to order. A royal inquisition post mortem was taken only for a TENANT-IN-CHIEF of the Crown. The Swonhungers held of the LORD BERKELEY by knight service and suit of court, and the Berkeleys held in chief — the calendars say so in their own entries, “held of the heir of William de Berkeleye in chief”. A mesne tenant's death produced no royal inquisition. So Smyth's “Inqu: 22. R. 2. p'. morte Johis Swonhunger” is very unlikely to be a Chancery IPM at all: it will be an inquisition taken in the Berkeley hundred court, or a document in the castle muniments Smyth had on his desk as steward. Look for it at Berkeley, not at Kew.
rows.why: THE CITATION IS REAL; THE REPOSITORY WAS WRONG
rows.file: TESTED 15 September 2026. The OCR of these volumes is poor — it prints Eohert for Robert and MTlliam for William — so the null was taken on fragment searches tolerant of that, not on exact spellings.

rows.what: PROB 11/1056/294 — the will of BENJAMIN COTTON, cordwainer of Berkeley, 1779
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew — digitised, and free with a free TNA account.
rows.cost: free, with a free TNA account
rows.settles: CATHERINE COTTON married Thomas Saniger at Berkeley on 10 April 1769 and was buried there on 27 September 1778. Eleven months after her burial a Benjamin Cotton, cordwainer, of the same small parish, has his will proved. Her father is given by the tree as EDWARD Cotton, so Benjamin is not him — but a Berkeley Cotton making a will in 1779 is well placed to name her, her widower or her children, and this archive has never had a document from her side of the family at all.
rows.why: THE FIRST COTTON DOCUMENT THIS ARCHIVE HAS FOUND
rows.file: Found 14 September 2026 in TNA Discovery. Speculative as to relationship, cheap to test, and free to read.

rows.what: The marriage certificate of JAMES SNEYD and ANN BIDDULPH, Stoke St Peter, 1842
rows.where: Stoke-on-Trent Register Office, against the local reference 31/03/214 found in the free Staffordshire index on 15 September 2026 — not the GRO.
rows.settles: BOTH FATHERS' NAMES AND OCCUPATIONS. This archive has James Sneyd the engraver across four censuses at Well Street, Hanley, and his wife appears in every one of them as “Ann” and nothing else. The index gives her BIDDULPH; the certificate would give her father, and carry this line back a generation on a side it has never had.
rows.why: THE ONLY SNEYD MARRIAGE THIS FAMILY LEFT IN ENGLAND AFTER 1837
rows.file: Found 15 September 2026. Their eldest, Elizabeth Ann, was born in 1839, three years before the wedding.

rows.what: Gloucestershire Archives D5555/2/9 — one bundle transcribing Men and Armour 1608, the hearth taxes of 1664 and 1672, and the poll tax of 1678
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives, Gloucester. Not digitised; a search room visit or a paid copy.
rows.settles: Whether a Saniger or Swonhunger household appears in the Vale between the muster of 1608 — which this archive has read, and which gave eleven men — and the parish registers. It is the single most efficient reference found on 15 September: three sources, one shelfmark.
rows.why: The 1608 muster names eleven men and then the trail goes quiet for a century and a half. A hearth tax names householders; a poll tax names adults. Either would put a name in a parish in a year.

rows.what: E 179/329 — Gloucestershire hearth tax, 1670–1674, about four hundred exemption certificates
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew. Not digitised — a visit, or a paid copying order.
rows.settles: Exemption certificates name the poor, which is precisely the half of a parish that leaves no other record. The catalogue says the bundle «includes names of individuals».
rows.why: Gloucestershire Archives holds a photostat of the enrolment as D383/1 with a part transcript, so the Gloucester copy may be the cheaper route to the same names.

rows.what: The court rolls of the manor of AWRE — WITHDRAWN, the premise was mine and not the record's
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives, Gloucester: D2156/1–4 (single surrenders of 1387, 1439, 1573 and 1577/8), D421/M7 (1588–91, with the Hundred of Bledisloe for 1591), D3270/362 (1671 and then nearly continuous to 1881) and D3270/363 (Awre and Etloe, 1760–1886).
rows.settles: WITHDRAWN 15 September 2026. This errand asked whether «the Sanigers of Awre and Blakeney» could be followed through the gap. **There are no Sanigers of Awre and Blakeney.** No record in this archive places the surname in the Forest of Dean; the 1608 muster puts all eleven men in Berkeley, Wotton, Dursley, Stroud and Stonehouse. Bigland's second volume mentions Awre 172 times and names no Saniger. The rolls are real and richly documented — 1387 to 1881 — and they are not about this family. Kept rather than deleted, as correction 32.
rows.why: Awre is not in FreeREG, has no surviving Protestation return, and is not covered by the 1381 poll tax membranes that survive. The court rolls are the one dense, continuous, surviving source for the parish — and they have never been asked.

rows.what: MS 3549/89 — the court roll of the manor of HAM AND HINTON, 1587–88, in John Smyth's own collection
rows.where: Library of Birmingham, Archives and Collections. Not digitised. MS 3549/182, a copy court roll of Alkington in 1624, is in the same series.
rows.cost: a visit, or a copying order
rows.settles: Who held land in Hinton fourteen years before JOHN SANIGER OF SANIGER appears in the Berkeley estate deeds of 1601, and twenty-one years before the muster of 1608 names eleven men of the surname. A court baron records surrenders, admissions and the deaths since the last court — which is a list of tenants with their heirs.
rows.why: It is the closest surviving document to the moment this family becomes visible, and it is in the wrong county to be found by anybody searching Gloucestershire. It exists at Birmingham because John Smyth of Nibley collected it while writing the very book this archive quotes.

rows.what: The will of EDWARD SANNIGER, mariner of Chepstow, proved at Llandaff 28 November 1806
rows.where: Two copies. LL/1806/24 at the National Library of Wales — digitised, but its catalogue is behind a bot check this archive will not complete. IR 26/352/152 at Kew is the Estate Duty abstract of the same will.
rows.cost: free at NLW if you open it yourself; a copying fee at Kew
rows.settles: Whether there is a Saniger branch across the Severn. He is a mariner at Chepstow, twenty miles by water from the Saniger fisheries on the Berkeley shore, spelling his name the way EDWARD SANNIGER OF BERKELEY, GENT spelled it in 1694. A will names family; the catalogue names nobody.
rows.why: Nothing yet connects him to this family beyond a surname, a spelling and a stretch of river. That is a hypothesis, and a will is the cheapest way to kill or confirm it.

rows.what: The will of THOMAS SANNIGER, Able Seaman of HMS Eurydice, 24 February 1794
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew — ADM 48/84/222, ship's pay book number 193.
rows.settles: Seamen's wills are short and almost always name next of kin — a wife, a mother, a brother — because that is what they exist to do. The catalogue gives his rank, his ship and nothing else.
rows.why: Found in the Discovery sweep of 15 September. Like the Chepstow mariner, he is a surname and a hypothesis until somebody reads the document.

rows.what: The 1774 conveyance of SANIGER FARM from Edward Saniger to the Earl of Berkeley
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives, most likely in D2957/41 — the Berkeley estate deeds, which already hold Edward Saniger's mortgages of 1692, 1709 and 1716 and the 1791 conveyance of the Great and Little Horse Marsh at Saniger.
rows.cost: a catalogue search, then a copy or a visit
rows.settles: **Whether this family held its own hamlet continuously from the thirteenth century to 1774.** J. H. Cooke asserted it in print in 1882 and this archive has graded the assertion INFERRED, because a conclusion in a journal is evidence of a scholar's reasoning, not of the fact. The deed itself would move it to documented — or break it.
rows.why: It is the single document that would close the gap this archive has called unbridgeable all week. Cooke had the Berkeley muniments in front of him; the conveyance he is describing should be in the estate papers the Earl received it into.

rows.what: The Tudor lay subsidy assessments for BERKELEY hundred — E 179/114/240, /235, /296/5, /272, /295
rows.where: The National Archives, Kew. Not digitised, no free published edition. The BLEDISLOE pieces named in the first version of this errand have been dropped: that hundred covers Awre, where this archive has no Sanigers at all (correction 32).
rows.cost: a visit, or a copying order
rows.settles: Whether anyone of this surname was taxed in **Berkeley hundred** in the 1540s — sixty years before the muster of 1608 found three men of the name in that hundred alone, at Halmore, Hinton and Saniger, and fifty before John Saniger appears in the estate deeds of 1601.
rows.why: Every piece is described as «Assessment (individuals)» — named taxpayers. It is the densest surviving named source for the hundred between the medieval deeds and the parish registers.

rows.what: Berkeley's settlement examinations and removal orders, Gloucestershire Quarter Sessions and parish chest
rows.where: Gloucestershire Archives. The Quarter Sessions are the Q series and the parish records the P series; NEITHER is catalogued by name, so this cannot be searched from here at all.
rows.settles: A settlement examination is a sworn statement of where a person was born, who their parents were, where they were apprenticed and whom they married — **the one record that names a labourer's parents**. The 1608 muster puts eleven men of this surname at the bottom of the Vale's scale: labourers and weavers of «lower stature». That is precisely the class the settlement papers exist to describe.
rows.why: Nothing else reaches these people. They leave no wills, no monuments and no deeds; the parish register gives a name and a date and no parentage.
rows.file: Gloucestershire Archives, Q and P series

rows.what: The court roll of the manor of Ham, 26 May 42 Elizabeth (1600)
rows.where: Berkeley Castle Muniments. Discovery itemises the BCM deeds but NOT the court rolls, so the roll is reachable only by asking the castle directly.
rows.cost: a written request, and probably a visit
rows.settles: Cooke read it in the 1880s and quotes the homage presenting the death of Nicholas Thorpe, «who died seised of the manor of Wanswell… and by keeping one tower in the Castle of Berkeley called Thorpe's Tower». A court baron lists the whole homage — the tenants of the manor — **one year before John Saniger first appears in the Berkeley estate deeds in 1601**.
rows.why: It is the closest surviving document to the moment this family becomes visible on the Berkeley side, and a named antiquary has already read it and said what is in it.
rows.file: BCM — Ham manor court roll, 42 Eliz.

ydna.what: A Y-DNA test from a male D'Arcy
ydna.settles: The Y chromosome descends father to son essentially unchanged. A male-line D'Arcy's would place this family against every other tested D'Arcy in the world — the most direct attack anyone can make on Robert D'Arcy's parentage, and it beats every archive visit on this page.
ydna.note: The descendant who has tested is female and has no Y chromosome. Her brothers do.

close: Several of these will come back empty. That is a result, and it belongs on the search register rather than in a drawer — so that the next person does not repeat it.

answered: asked and settled — kept because the answer is the finding
open: waiting on a visit, a fee or a sign-in this archive will not make

tallyNote: Eight of these were resolved and said so only by shouting in the prose. They now carry a state, so the count is a number rather than a reading exercise — the same reason [the work list](/worklist/) exists.
